summary: One of the best-known atheists talks with the historian whose book *Dominion* argues that the modern West, including its secular values, was shaped by Christianity. They range over the shock of the crucifixion in the Roman world, Paul's letters, the Good Samaritan, Islam, and whether secular societies are living off moral capital they no longer recognise.
insight: Holland's core claim, set out in *Dominion*, is that values most Westerners treat as simply obvious, such as concern for the weak and the equal worth of every person, would have looked strange to the ancient world and reached us through Christianity. Listen for how Harris, an atheist, responds: does a faith's influence on history tell us anything about whether it is true?
question: If your deepest values came from a faith you don't share, does that matter? Can they survive without it?

live.title: Trace a value home
live.text: Pick one value you hold deeply, such as compassion or equality. This week, ask where you first learned it, and from whom.

summary: The New Testament scholar Bart Ehrman describes his path from born-again Christian to agnostic, and talks with Harris about the historical Jesus, miracles, how the Bible was written, the resurrection, heaven and hell, and how Christianity changed after the emperor Constantine.
insight: Ehrman is a useful honest sceptic: he is confident that Jesus existed and was crucified, and that his followers sincerely believed they had seen him alive again, while arguing that historians as historians cannot conclude a miracle happened. Listening to him alongside N.T. Wright shows exactly where history ends and faith begins.
question: What would it take for you to believe the resurrection happened? What would it take to rule it out?

live.title: Read the account yourself
live.text: Read Luke 24 this week, slowly. Write down your honest response, whatever it is.

summary: Peterson talks with the Oxford mathematician John Lennox about how faith, reason and evidence fit together in science, about the dream of transhumanism to upgrade human beings with technology, and about the difference between humble, courageous inquiry and the proud ambition to make ourselves gods.
insight: Lennox argues that science itself rests on faith of a kind: trust that the universe is rationally intelligible, which he sees as pointing to a rational creator. On transhumanism, both warn that the attempt to engineer a 'better' human can forget what a human being is for.
question: Is wanting to overcome every human limit an ambition, or a temptation?

live.title: Set one limit
live.text: Set one limit on technology this week: one phone-free meal every day.

episode: The Science of Gratitude & How to Build a Gratitude Practice
summary: The neuroscientist Andrew Huberman reviews research on gratitude and argues that the usual advice, listing things you're thankful for, is not the most effective. A short practice built around a real story of gratitude, repeated a few times a week, works better.
insight: Huberman's suggestion is to recall a genuine story, either of being sincerely thanked or of watching someone else receive heartfelt thanks, and spend a few minutes feeling into it. That is strikingly close to the evening Examen, which begins not with a list but with remembering the particular gifts of the day and the people behind them.
question: Who thanked you, or whom did you see thanked, in a way that moved you? Take a minute with that story tonight.

live.title: A story of gratitude
live.text: Three times this week, spend two minutes recalling a real story of gratitude, then do your evening Review.

episode: Alex O'Connor and Glen Scrivener on Christianity and morality
summary: In Justin Brierley's new show, which pairs thinkers who disagree, the agnostic podcaster Alex O'Connor and the Christian writer Glen Scrivener, author of *The Air We Breathe* (2022), take on Christianity and morality.
insight: Scrivener's book argues that the values we breathe in without noticing, like compassion, equality and consent, come from Christianity. O'Connor has long pressed the question of whether a value's historical origin says anything about its truth. Listen for where that disagreement lands.
question: Is it enough that a value is good, or does it matter where it came from?

live.title: Live an inherited value
live.text: Choose one good value you inherited. Act on it deliberately once each day this week.

episode: Is God's hiddenness proof he isn't there? Live Debate Theist Dr Max Baker-Hytch vs Atheist Dr Julian Baggini
summary: A live debate between the atheist public philosopher Julian Baggini and the Christian philosopher Max Baker-Hytch of Oxford University on the problem of divine hiddenness: if God exists and loves us, why is his existence not obvious to everyone?
insight: The debate turns on whether God's apparent absence is better explained by his non-existence or by reasons a loving God might have for not overwhelming us. Listen for how each side treats history, personal experience, and the fact that belief seems shaped by culture and upbringing.
question: If God exists, what reasons might he have for not making himself more obvious, and are any of them good enough?

live.title: Seek honestly
live.text: Each night this week, say honestly, 'If you are there, show me.' Write down one thing from the day that you are grateful for, without forcing any conclusion.

summary: The historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook turn to the most mysterious figure of all: who Jesus was, what he taught, and whether he existed at all. This is the first part of a two-part conversation; the second is for members only.
insight: Holland, author of *Dominion*, and Sandbrook come to Jesus as working historians rather than as theologians or debaters. Listen for how they weigh the sources, the Gospels and the few outside writers, and where they draw the line between what history can say and what is a matter of faith.
question: What evidence would you accept for any other person from the ancient world, and do you hold Jesus to the same standard?

live.title: Weigh one source
live.text: This week, read Mark 1 and Josephus's two passages on Jesus side by side. Write one line on what each tells you, and one on what neither can.

show: Unbelievable? with Justin Brierley (Premier Christian Radio)
episode: The problem of suffering - Ehrman & Swinburne
summary: The New Testament scholar Bart Ehrman, who lost his Christian faith over the problem of suffering, sets out the case of his book *God's Problem*: the Bible gives several different explanations for suffering, and none of them convinces. The Oxford philosopher Richard Swinburne replies with the arguments of his own book, *Providence and the Problem of Evil*, that a good God could allow suffering for the sake of goods that could not exist without it.
insight: This is the problem of suffering argued live by two of its best-known voices, a scholar of the Bible and a philosopher of religion. Ehrman later wrote that it was the only radio debate in which he got genuinely angry, because the answers felt remote from real pain. Listen for both the arguments and the tone: can suffering be discussed in the abstract without wronging those who suffer?
question: Which matters more to you in a reply to suffering: that it is logically sound, or that it could be said to someone in pain?

live.title: Ask, don't argue
live.text: This week, ask one person who has been through real suffering what helped them and what didn't. Listen, and offer no explanation of your own.

episode: Kate Bowler — On Being in a Body
summary: Kate Bowler, a Duke historian of Christianity known for her study of the American prosperity gospel, talks with Krista Tippett about her Mennonite upbringing and about living for years with Stage IV colon cancer, diagnosed at 35. They discuss the gap between medical statistics and life in a body, different kinds of time, touch, hope without certainty, and writing blessings for lives that did not go to plan.
insight: Bowler had studied a gospel that promises health and wealth to the faithful, and then her own diagnosis put every such promise to the test. What she offers is not an explanation but a way of living honestly inside an unfinished story, and of noticing other people's pain because of your own.
question: What would hope look like for you if it did not depend on things turning out well?

live.title: Write a blessing
live.text: This week, write a few honest lines of blessing for someone whose life has not gone to plan, without promising them it will be fixed. Give it to them, or keep it and pray it.

episode: What happens when we die? NT Wright on the Afterlife and NDEs
summary: The New Testament scholar N.T. Wright and his fellow scholar Michael Bird answer listeners' questions. They take up near-death experiences: whether they are real, whether they give a glimpse of an afterlife, and how cautious we should be about them. They also talk about living faithfully in ordinary work, and about who has authority to forgive sins.
insight: Wright is best known for arguing, in Surprised by Hope (2008), that the Christian hope is not mainly about going to heaven when you die but about resurrection and a renewed creation. Listen for whether he keeps apart two questions people often merge: what may happen to us straight after death, and what the Bible finally promises.
question: If someone told you they had glimpsed the other side, what would it take for you to believe them? Would it change what you hope for?

live.title: Ask the question aloud
live.text: This week, ask one friend or relative what they think happens when we die. Listen to the whole answer before you give yours.

summary: In this episode, first broadcast in 2019 and re-released in 2024, the New Testament scholar and former Bishop of Durham Tom Wright answers listeners' questions about prayer. If God already knows what we need, what is the point of asking? Can a Christian claim 'anything' by praying in Jesus's name, as some read the Gospels to promise? He also talks about his own habits and ways of praying.
insight: These are the questions every beginner asks, and they sit right inside the Gospels: Jesus tells his friends to keep asking, and also says the Father knows what they need before they ask. Hearing a leading scholar take them seriously, and then describe how he actually prays, is a reminder that prayer is learned by doing as much as by thinking.
question: If God already knows what you need, why might it still matter that you ask?

live.title: Ask plainly
live.text: Each day this week, ask God for one specific thing you need, in a single sentence, and write it down with the date. At the end of the week, read the list back slowly.

episode: #159 What difference does prayer make? Tom shares his prayer habits
summary: Tom Wright takes listeners' questions about whether prayer works and how to do it. Is prayer just telling God what to do? What difference can it make if God has already decided what will happen? One listener is anxious about praying aloud before meals in public; another is uneasy about showy public prayer in America. Wright also describes his own practice, including keeping a prayer diary.
insight: The questions move from the philosophical to the very ordinary, and that is the point: whether prayer changes anything is not only a puzzle about God's plans but a matter of what we actually do at a café table or in a notebook. A prayer diary is a simple way to notice, over time, what has happened, without forcing an answer.
question: What would you need to see to believe prayer makes a difference, and is that the only kind of difference that counts?

live.title: Keep a prayer diary
live.text: This week, write down each day the people and situations you pray for, with the date. Leave a space beside each one. In a month, look back and note honestly what changed, in them or in you, and what did not.

summary: On Christmas Day the historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook ask whether Christmas is really Christian or borrowed from older festivals. They test the popular claims one by one: that the god Mithras was born on 25 December, that Christmas grew out of the Roman Saturnalia, and that the Church took the date from a feast of the Unconquered Sun.
insight: They find no ancient evidence for the Mithras claims, note that Saturnalia and Christmas were kept side by side as separate festivals, and favour the view that early Christians reached 25 December by their own reckoning, nine months after the date they gave to Christ's conception, 25 March. Listen for the twist: the idea that Christmas is pagan was pressed hardest not by modern sceptics but by Puritans who wanted it abolished.
question: If a Christian feast did take over an older custom, does that empty it of meaning, or show that it answers something people were already reaching for?

live.title: Trace one custom
live.text: Choose one custom you keep at Christmas or Easter, a tree, an egg, a carol, and find out where it really comes from. Tell someone what you learned, and keep the custom with that in mind.

episode: How to Use Music to Boost Motivation, Mood & Improve Learning
summary: In a solo episode, the neuroscientist Andrew Huberman explains how the brain and body respond to music: how it shifts mood, heart rate and motivation, how the brain predicts and rewards musical surprise, why 'sad' music can help people work through sadness rather than deepen it, and how playing an instrument or singing changes the brain.
insight: Huberman treats music as a tool you can use on yourself, which is the sharpest form of the sceptic's case: if a playlist can reliably lift your mood, perhaps a choir in a cathedral is doing the same thing with better acoustics. Listen for what his account explains well, and for what it leaves out, such as why people care whether the words they sing are true.
question: Is there a piece of music you use to change how you feel? Does knowing how it works spoil it for you?

live.title: Listen without using it
live.text: Once this week, listen to one piece of sacred music from start to finish while doing nothing else, not to change your mood but to attend to it. Write one line about what you heard.

episode: Dacher Keltner — The Thrilling New Science of Awe
summary: Dacher Keltner, a psychologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who helped found the modern study of awe, talks with Krista Tippett about the research behind his book Awe (2023). They discuss a study that gathered about 2,600 accounts of awe in 20 languages, the everyday kinds of wonder it found, among them moral beauty, shared ritual, nature and the spiritual, and what awe seems to do to the body and to our sense of self.
insight: The surprise in Keltner's research is that people most often found awe not in mountains or the night sky but in other people's courage, kindness and strength. Listen for how close that comes to an old idea in both Plato and the Bible: that goodness is itself a kind of beauty.
question: Whose goodness has filled you with awe, and did you ever tell them?

live.title: Name the goodness you see
live.text: This week, when you see someone act with courage or kindness, tell them in a sentence, the same day, what you saw.

episode: John O'Donohue — The Inner Landscape of Beauty
summary: The Irish poet, philosopher and theologian John O'Donohue, author of Anam Cara and of a book on beauty, talks with Krista Tippett about beauty as a human calling, the Celtic sense of an invisible world woven through the visible one, and the inner landscape of the soul. It was one of the last interviews he gave before his sudden death in 2008, and On Being describes it as the most loved conversation the programme has made.
insight: O'Donohue will not let beauty shrink to prettiness. For him it is 'that in the presence of which we feel more alive', and it asks something of us: a fuller way of becoming. Listen for how close this is to Diotima's ladder, and for what a Christian poet adds that Plato did not have.
question: Where in your week do you feel most alive, and is beauty part of it?

live.title: Look together
live.text: This week, spend fifteen minutes with someone you love looking properly at one beautiful thing, a painting, a view from a window, a piece of music, and then tell each other what you each saw.
